title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 15: Cruz v. Secretary of Environment -- IPRA: Social Justice or Reverse Discrimination?
keywords: IPRA: Social Justice or Reverse Discrimination?
primary_topics: Chapter 15 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's analysis of Cruz v. Secretary of Environment (GR 135385, December 6, 2000, per curiam), the constitutional challenge to the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 (IPRA, RA 8371), which a 7-7 deadlocked Court dismissed for failure to obtain a majority

The core controversy: whether IPRA's grant to indigenous cultural communities/indigenous peoples (ICCs/IPs) of 'ownership' over ancestral domains and ancestral lands -- including bodies of water, minerals and natural resources -- violates the Regalian doctrine (State ownership of natural resources under Section 2, Article XII of the Constitution), framed as 'social justice or reverse discrimination?'

The split opinions: Justice Kapunan (joined by Davide, Bellosillo, Quisumbing, Santiago) and Justice Puno upholding IPRA on the theory of 'native title' (Cariño v. Insular Government) and a distinct 'private but community' indigenous concept of ownership; against Justices Panganiban and Vitug (joined by Melo, Pardo, Buena, Gonzaga-Reyes, De Leon) voting to strike down key provisions; with Mendoza dismissing on standing alone

CJP's Separate Opinion: that IPRA unconstitutionally grants ownership and control over public-domain lands and natural resources to a minority -- concentrating roughly a third of Philippine territory and 80% of mineral resources in about 12 million people (110 ICCs) versus 60+ million others -- amounting to 'reverse discrimination,' though he concedes the constitutionality of PRIORITY and preferential use and small-scale utilization (Section 57)
sub_topics: The petitioners and the deadlock: former Justice Isagani A. Cruz and Cesar Europa challenged IPRA's constitutionality; the Court split 7 to dismiss and 7 to grant (only 14 voting, Justice Purisima having retired), so the petition was dismissed under Rule 56, Section 7 for want of a majority -- an 'indecisive Decision' Cruz himself lamented in his Inquirer column

The indigenous peoples' historic grievance: marginalized 'since time immemorial,' their claim of ownership antedating the Spanish conquistadores, captured in Kalinga chieftain Macli-ing Dulag's cry -- 'How can you own that which will outlive you? Only the race owns the land'

The challenged provisions: IPRA's definitions and grants of ancestral domains/lands (Sections 3, 5, 6, 7, 8), priority rights over natural resources (Section 57), NCIP powers and jurisdiction (Sections 51-53, 59, 63, 65, 66), and the characterization of the NCIP's relationship to the Office of the President -- attacked under the Regalian doctrine and the due-process and presidential-control clauses

The Kapunan opinion (upholding IPRA): grounded in Cariño v. Insular Government -- a claim of ownership 'since time immemorial' is an exception to jura regalia; existing rights are protected across the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions; customary law is constitutionally sanctioned (Section 5, Article XII); IPRA does NOT bestow ownership of natural resources (which 'belong to the State') but recognizes native title to LAND, with NCIP jurisdiction extending to lands, not resources

The Puno opinion (upholding with exceptions): ICCs/IPs hold a 'distinct kind of ownership' acquired by native title (or torrens for ancestral lands), formalized in a Certificate of Ancestral Domain Title (CADT); ancestral domains are 'private but community property' that cannot be alienated, outside the public domain; but the Implementing Rules' grant of 'ownership over natural resources' is unconstitutional, the rights being only 'stewardship'/small-scale utilization plus priority in large-scale development under State control (the State's four options under Section 57)

CJP's Separate Opinion (striking down): IPRA recognizes or grants ownership over lands of the public domain, waters and natural resources that 'are owned by the State' and 'shall not be alienated' (Section 2, Article XII), and defeats the State's constitutionally required 'full control and supervision' of natural resources; the Regalian doctrine, embedded since the 1935 Charter, vests the patrimony in all the Filipino people

CJP's 'reverse discrimination' argument: ancestral domains could cover about a third of Philippine territory and 80% of its mineral resources, concentrating the nation's wealth among roughly 12 million people (110 ICCs) to the exclusion of 60+ million other Filipinos -- violating the constitutional principle of 'more equitable distribution of opportunities, income, and wealth'; 'peace cannot be attained by brazenly and permanently depriving the many in order to coddle the few'

CJP's conception of social justice: the law should 'help the powerless by enabling them to take advantage of opportunities... open to all and by preventing the powerful from exploiting' them -- 'empowering and enabling the poor to be equally able to compete with the rich,' NOT granting a minority perpetual exclusive ownership of the national patrimony

What CJP concedes: he supports according ICCs/IPs PRIORITY and preferential use of ancestral lands and small-scale utilization of natural resources (consistent with Section 57 and the third paragraph of Section 2, Article XII), objecting only to perpetual exclusive OWNERSHIP and control; he reserves judgment on collateral issues (private-land inclusion, taxation, NCIP composition, customary-law priority) pending proper cases

The Vitug opinion (striking down Sections 3(a), 7, 57): IPRA amounts to 'an undue delegation, if not an unacceptable abdication, of State authority' over a significant area and the patrimony; Cariño cannot 'override the collective will of the people expressed in the Constitution'; customary law must be codified and published (Tanada v. Tuvera) before binding -- and he urges Congress to re-examine the law

The Mendoza position: dismissal solely because the petition raised no justiciable controversy and petitioners lacked standing -- and Puno's comparative discussion of US 'aboriginal title' to American Indian lands, noting the State's retained power to extinguish such titles

stances.claim: IPRA is unconstitutional insofar as it recognizes or grants ICCs/IPs OWNERSHIP and control over lands of the public domain and natural resources, which under Section 2, Article XII 'are owned by the State' and 'shall not be alienated,' and whose exploration, development and utilization must be 'under the full control and supervision of the State.' Native title (Cariño) extends, at most, to the surface of ancestral LANDS -- not to the natural resources beneath -- and 'four hundred years of Philippine political history cannot be set aside' by a well-intentioned statute.
stances.rhetorical_move: Regalian-doctrine supremacy: anchoring the objection in the Constitution's State-ownership of natural resources and the historical continuity of jura regalia, while narrowing native title to land surfaces
stances.confidence: asserted firmly as CJP's constitutional position (the 7-vote view that did not prevail for want of a majority)

stances.claim: Granting a minority perpetual, exclusive ownership of roughly a third of Philippine territory and 80% of its mineral resources -- concentrating the patrimony among about 12 million people (110 ICCs) against 60+ million other Filipinos -- is 'reverse discrimination' that violates the constitutional aim of a 'more equitable distribution of opportunities, income, and wealth.' True social justice 'empowers and enables the poor to be equally able to compete with the rich,' not by 'permanently depriving the many in order to coddle the few.'
stances.rhetorical_move: social-justice-as-equal-empowerment: redefining social justice against perpetual exclusive entitlement, using the distribution-of-wealth clause to recast a pro-minority grant as inequitable

stances.claim: CJP nonetheless supports according indigenous peoples PRIORITY and preferential use of their ancestral lands and small-scale utilization of natural resources (consistent with Section 57 and the third paragraph of Section 2, Article XII); his objection is only to perpetual exclusive OWNERSHIP and control, not to preference -- 'I would concede giving them priority... But to grant perpetual ownership... would be not only unjust but also subversive of the rule of law.'
stances.rhetorical_move: priority-yes/ownership-no distinction: separating constitutionally permissible preferential use from impermissible perpetual ownership to show the objection is not hostility to indigenous welfare
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's qualified, sympathetic position

notable_anecdotes: Macli-ing Dulag's cry: CJP opens by quoting the Kalinga chieftain -- 'You asked if we own the land.... How can you own that which will outlive you? Only the race owns the land because only the race lives forever' -- to capture the indigenous peoples' anguish before turning to the constitutional problem.

The 7-7 'indecisive Decision': the Court deadlocked and dismissed the petition for want of a majority, prompting petitioner Isagani Cruz to wish in his Inquirer column that 'at least one of the justices had moved to one or the other side' to produce a decisive ruling -- the merits left 'hanging in the air.'

A third of the country, 80% of the minerals: CJP marshals the Solicitor General's estimate that ancestral domains could cover 80% of the nation's mineral resources and 8-10 million of its 30 million hectares, concentrating four-fifths of natural resources and a third of the land among about 12 million Filipinos in 110 ICCs.

The point of agreement: across all the opinions, CJP notes a 'general understanding that natural resources within ancestral domains were not bestowed by IPRA' on the indigenous peoples -- even Kapunan and Puno conceding State ownership of those resources -- so the deep divide was over LAND ownership and the reach of native title.

Vitug's plea to Congress: voting to strike down key sections as 'an unacceptable abdication of State authority,' Justice Vitug nonetheless granted that 'IPRA has several good points' and urged Congress to re-examine and properly codify the law rather than leave customary law to operate unpublished.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'A Centenary of Justice' analyzes Cruz v. Secretary of Environment (GR 135385, December 6, 2000, per curiam), the constitutional challenge to the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 (IPRA, RA 8371), which a 7-7 deadlocked Court dismissed for want of a majority -- an 'indecisive Decision' petitioner Isagani Cruz himself lamented. Opening with Kalinga chieftain Macli-ing Dulag's cry ('How can you own that which will outlive you? Only the race owns the land'), CJP frames the question as 'social justice or reverse discrimination?': whether IPRA's grant to indigenous cultural communities/indigenous peoples of 'ownership' over ancestral domains and lands -- including waters, minerals and natural resources -- violates the Regalian doctrine of State ownership under Section 2, Article XII. Seven justices voted to uphold: Justice Kapunan (joined by Davide, Bellosillo, Quisumbing, Santiago) grounded native title in Cariño v. Insular Government as an exception to jura regalia (while conceding natural resources belong to the State), and Justice Puno described a 'distinct... private but community' indigenous ownership formalized in a CADT, with resource rights limited to stewardship and small-scale use plus priority in large-scale development under State control. Seven voted to strike down: CJP's own Separate Opinion argued IPRA unconstitutionally grants ownership and control over public-domain lands and natural resources that 'are owned by the State' and 'shall not be alienated,' defeating the State's required 'full control and supervision'; that native title (Cariño) reaches at most the land surface, not the resources beneath; and that concentrating roughly a third of Philippine territory and 80% of its minerals among about 12 million people (110 ICCs) against 60+ million other Filipinos is 'reverse discrimination' offending the constitutional aim of a 'more equitable distribution of opportunities, income, and wealth.' Crucially, he concedes the constitutionality of PRIORITY, preferential use and small-scale utilization (Section 57), objecting only to perpetual exclusive OWNERSHIP -- his conception of social justice being to 'empower and enable the poor to be equally able to compete with the rich,' not to 'permanently deprive the many in order to coddle the few.' Justice Vitug likewise voted to strike down key sections as 'an unacceptable abdication of State authority,' urging Congress to re-examine and codify the law, while Justice Mendoza would have dismissed on standing alone.
